I'm not gonna say exclusive because the whole point of art is to speak to everyone to some degree or another but a recent exemple can be Kleber Mendonça Filho's *Bacurau*, as it holds many references to the contemporary Brazilian political climate and history. And more than that, it is a **very** Northeastern Brazilian piece of art that hit some Southern/Southeastern Brazilian audiences a bit hard.

*Retratos Fantasmas* by him, on the other hand, despite being a love letter to his city, Recife, feels much more comprehensive since any large city with an "abandoned" downtown district can relate to the story he tells.

there is an assamese(assamese is an indian language) film called mon jaai. long back, assam used to be under constant threat by terrorists who wanted to "free" assam. they basically wanted to make assam a sovereign nation. because of this and many other factors, lots of educated youth sat in their homes with no jobs. the movie perfectly encapsulates how assamese yoth felt in those days.

the movie is available on youtube but the quality is very very bad as the assamese film industry was still taking baby steps because despite some movies winning nationwide awards, nobody wanted to invest in assamese films as most movies were not made to suit the audience. the directors during those days used to make lots of art films. many of them have been lost but mon jaai is one of the few which are still available because it had gotten a dvd release

[Cosy Dens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosy_Dens) is considered by many to be the best Czech movie of all time, but that's *precisely* because it's just so damn perfect in portraying (and parodying) those specific little things about the lives of regular humans living under the communist regime in Czechoslovakia. Almost nothing is explicitly explained to the viewer at face value (there was no need, cause the movie was not aimed at the international market), so it's usually quite a strange experience for foreigners.   


If you've got a Czech or Slovak friend, I definitely recommend asking them to watch this with you. You can learn a lot about life in that era of Eastern Europe when they start explaining stuff to you.

I feel a certain closeness to the films of Paul Schrader due to my Calvinist, Dutch Reformed/fundamentalist upbringing. Obviously his works are accessible to wider audiences, but they all have a certain religious specificity that speaks to how I was raised. The brooding sense of original sin present in his characters, the moralizing, the lonely, isolating individualism. This is only significant because there simply aren’t many prominent filmmakers who deal with the Protestant ethos. I can think of only Schrader and Bergman off the top of my head.

For Spain you have the whole genre of "cine quinqui", based on the characters of mythical 80s Robin Hood sort of figures who would stick up a bank while also stealing the heart of a pretty cashier.

In reality they were mostly marginalised heroin addicts and criminals, but the genre is a testament to the craziness of the 80s, when our 40 year long nationalistic dictatorship fell and people suddenly found themselves with a whole lot of political freedom, as well as a flood of cheap, pure heroin brought in by the Marsellan connection (and some sectors of the police and government forces, in a similar way to how crack was introduced in restless black neighbourhoods).

I didn't live through it, but I like the genre (many famous flamenco songs were used or produced as soundtracks). My mother says back then some parts were like the wild west.

The acting is often very stiff and forced because they used the actual famous robbers as actors, or untrained people from the same neighbourhoods. What was lacking in technique was compensated with soul.

The same is true for eras, as well as for cultural backgrounds -- some films can be difficult to understand for those who weren't there. I grew up in NYC in the 70s and 80s. When discussing 70s NYC movies (like Serpico, or The French Connection) with my kids, it became clear to me they were thinking of them as slightly fantastical -- I had to say, "No actually it really WAS like that, I was there back then!"

There are also films that are the product of a particular political moment, and are incomprehensible outside of it. After watching All The President's Men one of my kids asked, "So, there was a time when it was a shocking idea that the US government might be corrupt?"  


Similarly incomprehensible political time-capsules are Godard's La Chinoise and Weekend, and Japanese lefitst films like Oshima's Night and Fog in Japan or Wakamatsu's Ecstasy of the Angels.

This isn't purely exclusive to my background, as I think a lot of people who live in rural communities will feel this, but **The Wicker Man**.

Until you've lived in a rural farming community you can't really understand how close knit they are and how easy it is for emotions to propagate through the community. 

In those types of communities in the UK you are bought up to look out for one another and to distrust anyone who wasn't born within 5 miles of you. It was very easy to understand how this small local village had settled on killing outsiders to protect their own needs.

How about something different:

*Meet Me In St Louis*

A beautiful, colorful happy musical starring Judy Garland at her height. The movie has no antagonist except the idea of moving away.

I'm a privileged white person that grew up in St Louis. Facing ever increasing crime and lowering job prospects, our family was one of the huge exodus that left it and other manufacturing cities from the 70s-90s. The movie encapsulates the feeling of losing the city we once loved and all the innocent joy we had there.

I recently discovered many people from socially different backgrounds as mine hate all musicals from the 30s-50s. They feel as if it's just peak white privilege to suspect worry and care when minority communities were going through so much pain in this eras. I'd never considered this before. Perhaps they have a point.
More mainstream but did *The VVitch* speak to you on those themes of original sin?

One genre of films that has been getting quite some spotlight lately is films centering around a first-generation East Asian immigrant protagonist - Past Lives, Turning Red, The Farewell, EEAAO to some degree.

The themes of alienation, family, identity are pretty universal, which is probably why these films have quite a lot of acclaim for the wider audience regardless. But there is a unique perspective of straddling between two different cultures and belonging to neither (or both?) that really hits home for me. There is also of a lot of subtext and jokes that requires a deep understanding of both cultures that really only comes from belonging in the center of this Venn diagram of demographic that I would say makes these films "exclusive" to a degree.

From my personal experience, I'd say we are more cynical, and like very surreal/absurd humor more than average. We also like catchphrases and puns a lot. 

Hungarians, in my opinion, also really like rude humor: a returning gag in Liza the Fox Fairy is a police character, who constantly tries to say proverbs, but forgets the end, and just says "kurva anyjat" instead. ("(his/hers/their) whore mother", common swearing/insult) I can never explain to my foreign friends why this is funny, but basically every Hungarian thinks it is. The Adventures of Ford Fairlane has such a cult following here, that even people who have never heard of the movie will quote some of the swearing from it.

I'm glad to hear recognition of Hungarian animation from abroad, I think we have some really unique stuff. If anyone is further interested, these are my recommendations:

\- Vuk (1981) - aforementioned story about a fox cub, adaptation of a famous Hungarian book. It is the most "conventional" movie on this list, so if you're only going to watch one, don't make it this one. Voice acting I think is pretty stellar.

\- Macskafogó (1986) - a cold-war esque spy story between mice and cats. Very enjoyable for adults as well

\- Any of the animated films of Marcell Jankovics, who mostly adapts classic Hungarian ballads, and sometimes folk tales. János vitéz (1973) and Fehérlófia (1981) are my personal favorites. These are also fairly enjoyable for adults as well, especially János vitéz has some pretty dark parts. He has a very strange, often surreal animation  style. If you're only going to watch precisely one Hungarian animated movie, I'd make it one of his. János vitéz is a more traditional folk tale in my opinion, Fehérlófia will probably feel weirder/more alien for foreign audiences.

\- The Hungarian Folk Tales (1980-2012) is maybe the most iconic of Hungarian animated television. It is what the title explains, traditional folk tales animated for kids mainly. You can find a lot of it on YouTube.

There are many more, that I could mention here, but these I feel are the most iconic/different from just generic animation you might see anywhere.
